stem: A 74-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of worsening difficulty swallowing solid foods and liquids, feeling as if food becomes 'stuck' in his throat. Over the past 6 months, he has noticed loud gurgling noises in his neck while eating, foul-smelling breath (halitosis), and frequent coughing spells when lying flat. Three days ago, he coughed up recognizable, undigested bits of dinner that he had eaten the previous evening. He has had two episodes of aspiration pneumonia treated with antibiotics over the past year. Physical examination reveals a soft, fluctuant, non-tender swelling on the left side of his neck that diminishes in size with manual compression, accompanied by a gurgling sound (Boyce sign). Barium swallow fluoroscopy demonstrates a 4-cm pouch protruding posteriorly from the hypopharynx immediately above the upper esophageal sphincter. Which of the following anatomical sites represents the precise area of muscular weakness through which this pouch herniated?

options.text: Laimer's triangle between the cricopharyngeus and circular longitudinal esophageal muscle fibers
options.explanation: Laimer's triangle (or area) is located inferior to the cricopharyngeus muscle, predisposing to rare Laimer diverticula, not classic Zenker pulsion diverticulum.

options.text: Killian-Jamieson space anterolateral to the esophagus below the insertion of the cricopharyngeus
options.explanation: The Killian-Jamieson space is located anterolaterally below the cricopharyngeus; herniation here creates a Killian-Jamieson diverticulum, which is lateral rather than posterior.

options.text: Pharyngobasilar fascia defect between the superior pharyngeal constrictor and the skull base
options.explanation: This defect (sinus of Morgagni) transmits the auditory (Eustachian) tube and levator veli palatini, not esophageal pulsion diverticula.

options.text: Killian's triangle between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor
options.explanation: ZENKER DIVERTICULUM is a FALSE (pulsion) diverticulum characterized by mucosal and submucosal herniation through a muscular defect in the posterior hypopharynx, known as KILLIAN'S TRIANGLE. Killian's triangle is an anatomical area of natural muscular weakness bounded superiorly by the oblique fibers of the THYROPHARYNGEUS muscle and inferiorly by the transverse fibers of the CRICOPHARYNGEUS muscle, both of which are components of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. The underlying pathophysiology is uncoordinated swallowing mechanics: increased intraluminal hypopharyngeal pressure during swallowing resulting from premature contraction or incomplete relaxation (spasm/incoordination) of the cricopharyngeus muscle (the upper esophageal sphincter). Over time, repeated high pulsion pressures force the hypopharyngeal mucosa and submucosa to herniate posteriorly through Killian's triangle. Because it lacks a muscularis propria layer, it is classified as a FALSE diverticulum. Clinical features include progressive oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, neck mass that gurgles on compression (Boyce sign), and a high risk of recurrent aspiration pneumonia. Treatment involves cricopharyngeal myotomy with diverticulectomy or endoscopic diverticulotomy.

options.text: Quadrangular membrane weakness between the aryepiglottic fold and vestibular ligament
options.explanation: The quadrangular membrane is an intrinsic laryngeal ligament forming the vestibular fold (false vocal cord), unrelated to hypopharyngeal pulsion diverticula.

stem: A 4-week-old first-born male infant is brought to the emergency department because of forceful vomiting after every feeding for the past 5 days. His mother states that the emesis shoots across the room ('projectile'), contains curdled milk without any green or yellow discoloration, and occurs immediately following breast milk feeding. Immediately after vomiting, the infant appears intensely hungry and eagerly attempts to feed again. Physical examination reveals a dehydrated infant with a sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and delayed capillary refill. Palpation of the abdomen reveals a firm, non-tender, mobile 2-cm olive-shaped mass in the right epigastrium, and visible peristaltic waves are seen moving from left to right across the upper abdomen. Serum electrolytes are: sodium 131 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, chloride 82 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 34 mEq/L. Which of the following physiological mechanisms directly drives the metabolic and urinary derangements in this infant?

options.text: Excessive duodenal bicarbonate loss into emesis with renal compensatory retention of hydrogen ions
options.explanation: Pyloric obstruction prevents duodenal contents from entering the stomach; emesis is non-bilious and loses gastric acid (H+ and Cl-), not alkaline duodenal secretions.

options.text: Failure of pancreatic alpha-amylase and bicarbonate secretion causing severe hyperchloremic non-gap metabolic acidosis
options.explanation: Pancreatic insufficiency does not cause projectile vomiting or metabolic alkalosis; HPS causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

options.text: Renal tubular loss of bicarbonate mediated by Fanconi syndrome with type 2 proximal RTA
options.explanation: Fanconi syndrome causes proximal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemic normal anion gap metabolic ACIDOSIS, not severe metabolic alkalosis with an epigastric olive mass.

options.text: Biliary free fatty acid wasting producing an unmeasured anion gap metabolic ketoacidosis
options.explanation: Fatty acid wasting causes malabsorption; the metabolic defect in HPS is a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic ALKALOSIS, not ketoacidosis.

options.text: Gastric hydrochloric acid loss causing intravascular contraction, secondary hyperaldosteronism, and paradoxical aciduria
options.explanation: This infant has INFANTILE HYPERTROPHIC PYLORIC STENOSIS (HPS), caused by hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle layer of the pylorus, producing gastric outlet obstruction. It characteristically manifests between 2 and 6 weeks of age, predominantly in first-born males, with non-bilious projectile vomiting, avid re-feeding hunger ('hungry vomiter'), peristaltic waves, and a palpable 'olive-like' mass in the epigastrium. Repeated vomiting of gastric secretions causes profound loss of GASTRIC HYDROCHLORIC ACID (H+ and Cl-) and water. The loss of H+ generates a severe METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (elevated serum bicarbonate). The loss of Cl- causes severe HYPOCHLOREMIA, which depletes luminal chloride in renal cortical collecting ducts, impairing pendrin (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) and preventing renal bicarbonate excretion. Concurrently, volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), driving SECONDARY HYPERALDOSTERONISM. Aldosterone acts on principal cells to reabsorb sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing HYPOKALEMIA. As systemic hypokalemia worsens, renal alpha-intercalated cells attempt to conserve potassium via the apical H+/K+ ATPase, pumping H+ ions into the urine despite existing systemic alkalemia. This phenomenon is termed PARADOXICAL ACIDURIA. Definitive correction requires initial IV volume and electrolyte repletion before surgical Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
